messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai had always been drawn to the most intense stories as a journalist, but nothing could have prepared him for the captivity he endured while reporting on a conflict in Eastern Europe. The memories of those three days still replayed like a film in his mind - the sound of footsteps outside his cell, the smell of cheap vodka wafting from his captors' breath, and the feeling of neck pain that radiated down his spine as he was forced to sit for hours on end. As Kai recalls these memories, they trigger an intense physical response. The mere thought of being touched sends a shiver down his spine, transporting him back to the moments when his captors would roughly handle him during interrogations. Even the smell of alcohol now makes him feel like he's reliving those terrifying moments. His neck pain, which began as a minor injury sustained during captivity, has become a constant reminder of the trauma he experienced. Kai's memories are no longer just recollections - they're an integral part of his threat monitoring system. Whenever he hears unexpected or loud sounds, he is instantly on high alert, convinced that danger lurks around every corner. The sound of a car backfiring outside his office window can send him into a panic, and he often finds himself reacting as if his life depends on it, even when nothing is actually wrong. As Kai becomes more hypervigilant, the memories of his captivity flood back, forcing their way into his mind uninvited. He can't escape the terror that accompanies these recollections - remembering the event brings back the same fear he felt at the time. It's as if the threat hasn't dissipated; it's just lying in wait, ready to pounce. Kai's work as a journalist has suffered as a result of his hypervigilance. He now avoids assignments that involve reporting from conflict zones or interviewing sources in person. Even simple tasks like walking down a busy street can become overwhelming, and he often finds himself scanning the surroundings for potential threats. His marriage is also starting to bear the strain - Kai's wife has grown frustrated with his constant need to be "on guard" and the way it affects their daily life. Despite trying to manage his symptoms on his own, Kai finally sought help when a particularly disturbing memory replay episode left him unable to work for several days. He hopes that therapy will help him learn to cope with these memories and reduce his threat monitoring system's constant chatter. What he fears most is losing himself in the process - becoming so consumed by the trauma of his past that he can no longer pursue the career or relationships he values. Kai's greatest hope is that, through treatment, he'll be able to find a way to quiet the memories and threats that have taken over his life. He wants to rediscover the journalist within himself - someone who can tell powerful stories without being haunted by the ghosts of his own past.
